pass_a_gloss:
They see clearly, naming a multitude of nations. They rushed upon the regions, or the cities of Judaea, like much water and like force carried, and making noises, but not like the sea, those opposing, being overwhelmed. He calls their back a multitude of nations among these, because many nations are pursued by them. They run after the back of all and in every way those fleeing, the pursuers. What then after this? He will send them backward, that is, he will send them behind, and he will pursue them from afar, like chaff of a threshing floor, those winnowing, before the wind, and like dust of a chariot, a stormy wind bearing. For what is thus easily blown away, like dust from a wheel and a threshing floor, a violent wind blowing? That Sennacherim, a fugitive, departed, the God of all will speak to him through the voice of Isaiah, saying: 'I will put a bridle in your mouth, and a bit in your lips, and I will turn you back on the way you came.' In the evening there will be mourning before morning, and it will not be. This is the portion of those who pasture you, and the inheritance of those who inherit you. Having spoken earlier, I said that Rhapsakes, having encircled Jerusalem with his army, and not having taken it far, having threatened, perished with his whole army before dawn and day. Mourning, therefore, will be, he says, in the evening, certainly, having expected in Jerusalem to be in the morning, and the war's attack, but it ceased before dawn. Through this he says: There will be mourning in the evening; it will not be before morning, that is, the weeping will cease and come to an end.

And at the same time, the ones from suffering will be driven out by fear, with God helping and having surprisingly destroyed the enemy's phalanxes and also having driven out the leader from Judea's land. This is what the blessed David explains, saying that in the evening there will be weeping, but in the morning, joy. This is the lot of those who have plundered and ravaged you, treating you as their own inheritance. He reproaches the Israelites because they have done what would have been expected to completely destroy the nation, but God pities it again and punishes with death those who ravage the people entrusted to him. For when the Most High divided the nations, as he scattered Adam's sons, he established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of God's angels, and the Lord's portion was his people, Jacob, the measuring line of his inheritance, Israel.
pass_b_english: The nations are clearly visible, and their multitude is named as they rush upon the regions, or the cities of Judaea, with a powerful and violent force, making noises and causing disturbances, much like a large body of water or a force carried with great momentum, but not like the sea, which overwhelms those who oppose it.
God calls their back a multitude of nations, because many nations are pursued by them, and the pursuers run after the backs of those who flee, doing so in every way and with great persistence.

What happens next is that God will send them backward, pursuing them from afar, much like chaff blown away by the wind, or like dust raised by a chariot, for what is easily blown away, like dust from a wheel or a threshing floor, by a violent wind, is indeed a pitiful sight.

Sennacherim, a fugitive, departed, and the God of all spoke to him through the voice of Isaiah, saying, 'I will put a bridle in your mouth, and a bit in your lips, and I will turn you back on the way you came' (Isaiah 30:28).
In the evening, there will be mourning, but it will not be before morning, that is, the weeping will cease and come to an end.
Earlier, it was said that Rhapsakes, having encircled Jerusalem with his army, and not having taken it far, having threatened, perished with his whole army before dawn and day.
Mourning, therefore, will be in the evening, certainly, because those in Jerusalem expected to be attacked in the morning, but the war's attack ceased before dawn.
Through this, God says that there will be mourning in the evening, but it will not last until morning, and the weeping will cease and come to an end.
As fear will drive out those who suffer, God will help, surprisingly destroying the enemy's phalanxes and driving out their leader from Judea's land.
The blessed David explains this, saying that 'in the evening we will weep, but in the morning, we will experience joy' (Psalm 30:5).
This is the lot of those who have plundered and ravaged God's people, treating them as their own inheritance.

God reproaches the Israelites because they have done what would have been expected to completely destroy the nation, but instead, he pities it again and punishes with death those who ravage the people entrusted to him.

For when the Most High divided the nations, as he scattered Adam's sons, he established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of God's angels, and the Lord's portion was his people, Jacob, the measuring line of his inheritance, Israel (Deuteronomy 32:8-9).
